1.pericope_label: Finally, my brethren, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not grievous, but for you it is safe. Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision. For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.

schools.summary: Ground the first epithet in the animals themselves, since eastern dogs are mostly masterless, wandering the streets and feeding on offal and even on corpses, and are held unclean, so that the word carries a contempt far stronger there than with us and had come to mean a man shameless, impudent, snarling and contentious; qualify the retort, since the party attacked claimed a special purity and were probably not impure, the opposite fault belonging to those censured at the end of the chapter; treat the third epithet as a coinage, a late word for incision or mutilation set against the ordinary word for circumcision, whose related verb appears in the Greek Old Testament only of forbidden cuttings; and gather the prophetic ground for transferring the name — the foreskin of the heart, the promise that the Lord will circumcise it — while correcting the reading to worship by the Spirit of God.

Read the claim as a transfer rather than an abolition: these are the true seed of Abraham and heirs of the covenant which the sign confirmed, because the real circumcision is inward and seated in the heart rather than visible in the flesh; supply the antithesis left implicit, that the false apostles pressed an outward worship and boasted of being God's people on the strength of keeping ceremonies; describe the inward work in stages, the heart pricked, its hardness removed, its iniquity laid open; and note from the Jewish side that the name of dog was the Jews' own term for Gentiles, now returned upon them, so that they should not find the severity strange given what their own sources say.

Render the coined third epithet as the cutting or excision, deliberately not the word for circumcision, and take it as degrading the pretension to sanctity that was made by cutting the flesh: the rite was honourable while it remained the sign of the covenant, but having rejected the new covenant their cutting is reduced to mere mutilation; and observe the reversal at work, that dog was the Jews' name for the Gentiles who stood outside the covenant, and that it is now turned on the Judaizing teachers themselves.

debates.question: Why is the name of dog turned back on the Judaising teachers?

sides.position: Because it was the Jews' own name for the Gentiles who stood outside the covenant, and is now returned upon them

Because by their wilful apostasy they now occupy the place outside the spiritual Israel that once belonged to the despised Gentiles — not because they were impure, since the party attacked claimed a special purity
Because the eastern dog is masterless, unclean and contentious, so the word is simply the strongest available contempt

debates.question: What is the coined third epithet?

sides.position: The cutting or excision, deliberately not the word for circumcision, degrading the pretension to sanctity made by cutting the flesh
A late noun for incision or mutilation set against the ordinary word for circumcision, whose related verb is used in the Greek Old Testament only of forbidden cuttings
Possibly drawn from the custom of posting a caution on a house guarded by a dog

outliers.note: Alone resists the obvious reading of the retort, observing that elsewhere the word marks the impure while the party attacked here claimed a special purity and were probably not impure at all, the opposite fault belonging to those censured at the end of the chapter.
Alone suggests the whole phrase may derive from the custom of posting a caution on a house guarded by a dog.

4.pericope_label: Though I might also have confidence in the flesh. If any other man thinketh that he hath whereof he might trust in the flesh, I more: Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee; Concerning zeal, persecuting the church; touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless. But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.

schools.summary: Read the catalogue as an argument rather than a boast, catching the logic of the opening, that more ground for confidence is claimed than the opponents have and then proved; take the eighth day as marking a Jew born rather than a proselyte, since Ishmaelites were circumcised in the thirteenth year and Gentile proselytes at mature age; make the tribe pointedly chosen, being the tribe of the first king whose name the apostle bore, the tribe holding the holy city, the one that stayed faithful when the rest fell away; explain a Hebrew descended from Hebrews as keeping the old tongue and customs wherever born and holding himself superior to the Hellenist; press the reversal as counting the whole loss not merely worthless but worse than worthless, since privilege prevents the sense of spiritual need; and keep the accounting metaphor plain, these being gains on the credit side of the ledger.

Preach the passage as a battlefield rather than a ledger, opening with the rule that in contests with heretics the attack must be made with minds in vigour so that exact attention can be given; then report that the heretics of the day sprang upon this very verse, arguing that if the law is called loss and refuse it cannot be of God; and explain the concealment as the wisdom of the Spirit, which suggests to them hopes of victory so that they will undertake the fight, since had the matter been spoken plainly they would have blotted out the words as they have done elsewhere — as with fishes, the hook that takes them is hidden so that they may swim up, and once they had taken it they were enclosed on all sides with nets.

Insist on the exactness rather than the bare fact of the rite, that the circumcision was performed duly and according to the appointment of the law, such customary circumcision being reckoned of superior value besides serving as a token of race, since foreigners were circumcised in youth or manhood or sometimes in old age; then locate the cause of the reversal rather than its effect, holding that ignorance of Christ is the sole reason we are puffed up with a vain confidence, so that wherever a false estimate of one's own excellence appears Christ is not known; and add that the moment Christ shines forth whatever had dazzled the eyes with a false splendour vanishes or is at least disesteemed, nothing having been so injurious as one's own righteousness.

Supply the textual detail behind the first item, that the law required the eighth day and that both the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek version preserve a clause, now lost from the common Hebrew text, cutting off the child not circumcised on that day; make the same point about the tribe from the other side, that it did not revolt with Jeroboam nor pollute the worship of God with idols; and describe concretely what the change cost, the credit and respect enjoyed as one zealously attached to the law and the traditions of the elders, together with what came to be seen, that no act of righteousness could be depended on for salvation.

debates.question: Why name the tribe of Benjamin?

sides.position: Because it was the tribe of the first king, whose name the apostle bore, the tribe to which the holy city belonged, and the one that stayed faithful when the rest fell away
Because it did not revolt with Jeroboam nor pollute the worship of God with idols

debates.question: What is being claimed by circumcision on the eighth day?

sides.position: That he was a Jew born and not a proselyte, since Ishmaelites were circumcised in the thirteenth year and Gentile proselytes at mature age
That the rite was performed duly and according to the appointment of the law, such customary circumcision being reckoned of superior value besides being a token of race
That the law's requirement was met, the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek version preserving a clause, now lost from the Hebrew text, cutting off the child not circumcised on that day

debates.question: In what sense were the gains counted loss?

sides.position: Not merely worthless but worse than worthless, because privilege prevents the sense of spiritual need that should bring a man to Christ
As things that had been hindrances, since ignorance of Christ is the sole reason we are puffed up with vain confidence and nothing was so injurious as his own righteousness
As entries moved from the credit to the debit side of a ledger, the man having been the star of hope for Gamaliel and the Sanhedrin

outliers.note: Alone treats the passage as a battlefield rather than a ledger, reporting that the heretics of his day seized on the words about loss and refuse as proof that the law is not of God, and that the apostle let them take the bait before enclosing them with his nets.
Alone reports that both the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint preserve a clause, lost from the common Hebrew text, cutting off the child not circumcised on the eighth day.

themes: what things were gain to me

8.pericope_label: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ, And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith: That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; If by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead.

schools.summary: Take the jettison figure literally, that the gains are regarded as sailors regard the goods on which they set a high value, willing to throw them all overboard to save themselves; handle the word rendered dung as a late term of uncertain etymology, either connected with a word for dung or from a phrase meaning to fling to the dogs, found in the papyri and occurring here only in the New Testament, and note the derivation from what is thrown to dogs would suit the retort of that name upon the Judaisers; count the five particles stacked before the sentence begins as showing the force and passion of the conviction; define the true righteousness first imperfectly as coming through faith and then completely as coming from God on the sole condition of faith; and set out the test, that many are willing to reign with Christ but not to suffer with him, to wear the crown of glory but not the crown of thorns.

Press the seaman's similitude and then withdraw part of it, since men who jettison cargo part with it regretfully and bewail the loss once ashore, whereas here the gains were held offensive; decline the passive that everyone else adopts in the ninth verse, arguing that the Greek, though passive in termination, carries an active signification meaning to recover what you have voluntarily given up, and adding the proverb that he had been lost if he had not been lost; hold that the two righteousnesses cannot stand together, since the law brings works while faith presents man naked before God; and distinguish two participations in the death of Christ, the inward mortification of the flesh and the outward endurance of the cross, so that the whole life must represent the image of death until it produce death itself.

Mark the escalation in the vocabulary, that loss is sustained with patience but dung is cast away with abhorrence, the word covering the vilest refuse of anything, the dross of metals, the dregs of liquors, the basest offals; narrow the fellowship of the sufferings carefully, since no creature can share the vicarious sufferings and the imitation intended is of Christ as a martyr to the truth; note the strong contemporary desire after martyrdom; and rest the last verse on the compound noun used here and nowhere else, reading it as the resurrection out from among the dead, perhaps peculiarly glorious in the case of martyrs.

Supply the images the others leave implicit: to be found in him is to be found as the manslayer was found in the city of refuge, safe from the avenger of blood, or else as a man is found of his Judge in peace; and set out plainly what is being laid hold of, that we are undone without a righteousness in which to appear before God, that the righteousness provided in Christ is complete and perfect, and that none have benefit by it but those who come off from confidence in themselves; then observe that the apostle was as ambitious of being sanctified as of being justified.

debates.question: Is the verb in the ninth verse passive or active?

sides.position: Active in signification though passive in termination, meaning to recover what you have voluntarily given up — he renounced everything in order to recover it in Christ
Passive, and best so read, though the active sense is true in substance since carnal privileges are exchanged for spiritual blessings
Passive, of being found in him at death or when Christ comes

debates.question: What does the word rendered dung mean?

sides.position: The vilest refuse of anything — dross of metals, dregs of liquors, the basest offals
Refuse of any kind, and possibly the fragments of a feast, the old derivation from what is thrown to dogs suiting the retort of that name earlier in the chapter
A late word of uncertain etymology, connected either with a term for dung or with a phrase meaning to fling to the dogs; found in the papyri and here only in the New Testament

debates.question: What is the resurrection aimed at in the eleventh verse?

sides.position: The resurrection out from among the dead, marked by a compound noun used here and nowhere else — not the general rising, which all will attain
The resurrection of the righteous as a thing to be secured by effort, not the common resurrection shared with all mankind

outliers.note: Alone declines the passive rendering of the verb in the ninth verse that every other commentator adopts, taking it as meaning to recover what one has voluntarily given up, and adding the proverb that he had been lost if he had not been lost.
Alone supplies the images the others leave implicit, that to be found in him is to be found as the manslayer was found in the city of refuge, safe from the avenger of blood.

themes: the excellency of the knowledge of Christ

12.pericope_label: Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

schools.summary: Take the denial of perfection as moral, a distinct assertion of not being free from sin, and ask who could urge better claims than this writer, concluding that whoever claims a holiness he did not pretend to shows little knowledge of himself — while reporting honestly that many critics refer the word instead to the games; add that no absolute perfection was known by any single experience and that attaining is one act while being perfected is a continuous process; observe that the metaphor of the race is broken deliberately, the eager runner stretching for the prize interrupted by the remembrance of having himself been grasped at his conversion by the hand of Christ; and note that the mark is Christ himself, the goal on which the eye stays fixed and which moves forward as we press on.

Unfold the race into three requirements: that it profits the runner nothing to have left the starting-point unless he goes forward to the goal, so that the calling must be pursued until death; that the way is marked out so that he need not tire himself wandering in this direction or that; and that he must be free from entanglement, surmounting every obstacle rather than stopping at it. Then raise the obvious objection, that recalling past mercies encourages hope and past sins prompt amendment, and answer that such thoughts do not turn the view backward but help the sight of the goal, what is condemned being only the looking back that destroys alacrity; and hold that the apostle did nothing except under Christ's influence and guidance.

Read the runner exactly: he reckons not how many circuits he has finished but how many are left, and the text does not say that reckoning them up is declined but that they are not even remembered; observe that the man who thinks all accomplished may cease running, as having apprehended all, while he who thinks himself still distant from the goal will never cease; warn that nothing so renders real excellences vain as remembering the good deeds we have done, since it makes us both remiss and haughty; and describe the stretching forward as a runner endeavouring to outstrip his own feet, throwing his body toward the front and reaching out his hands to gain a little more of the course.

Hold that the whole passage is one continued allusion to the contests at the games, running from the eleventh verse to the seventeenth, with which the readers were well acquainted; then press the verb for being perfected as the technical word for those who have completed their race and are honoured with the prize, documenting from Philo, from Clement of Alexandria defining it as the consummation of the work of charity rather than the end of life, and from Basil, Oecumenius and Eusebius, that it had come to mean martyrdom outright; conclude that no deficiency of grace is spoken of here and call the contrary opinion most falsely and dangerously imagined; and keep the mark to the stadium, the white line from start to goal which a runner who strayed beyond was not crowned for crossing first.

debates.question: What is denied by the words or am already made perfect?

sides.position: Moral perfection: this is a distinct assertion of not being free from sin, and whoever claims a holiness the apostle did not pretend to shows little knowledge of himself
Nothing about grace at all: the verb is the technical word for completing the race and had come to mean martyrdom outright, and the contrary opinion is most falsely and dangerously imagined
Absolute perfection by a single experience, the goal being still ahead and not behind
Attainment of full spiritual perfection on this side of the grave, attaining being a single act and being perfected a continuous process

debates.question: Is it right to look back at all?

sides.position: Only the looking back that destroys alacrity is condemned; recalling past mercies and past sins helps rather than hinders the sight of the goal
The precept is absolutely general, applying to past blessings, past achievements, and even past sins
Not even remembered, let alone reckoned up: the runner counts not the circuits finished but those left

debates.question: What is the mark pressed toward?

sides.position: The white line running from start to goal, which a runner who strayed beyond was not crowned for crossing first
Christ himself, the scope of all the counsels of God and of the covenant of grace
Jesus, on whom the runner must continually look, the goal moving forward as we press on yet never out of sight

outliers.note: Alone documents from Philo, Clement of Alexandria, Basil, Oecumenius and Eusebius that the verb for being perfected had come to mean martyrdom, and on that ground denies that any deficiency of grace is spoken of here.

Alone presses the exact wording, that the text does not say the past achievements are declined to be reckoned up but that they are not even remembered, and warns that remembering our good deeds makes us at once remiss and haughty.

themes: not as though I had already attained
forgetting those things which are behind
the prize of the high calling

15.pericope_label: Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.

schools.summary: Weigh the address to the perfect as ironical, aimed at those who held themselves already to have attained, and draw out the paradox that such men are bidden to prove their perfection by a consciousness of imperfection, so that if they lack it they have something yet to learn; or else take the term as relative perfection in contrast to the absolute perfection just denied, including the writer among the spiritual adults; hesitate over the address itself and prefer to read it as those who would be perfect or are aiming at it, since he can hardly call them what he had refused to call himself; note that such cases are simply turned over to God; and report the textual state of the following verse, where the oldest witnesses lack the word for rule.

Make the promise of further revelation do double work, humbling the readers and giving them good hope at once: they are admonished not to be elated in their ignorance and at the same time told to take courage, since a man must make way for the revelation of God if he has not yet attained what he seeks, obstinacy being the great obstacle to truth, so that the best preparation for docility is not to take pleasure in error; draw the pastoral inference that we must bear for a time with ignorance in weaker brethren and forgive them if it is not given them at once to be of one mind with us; observe that the Greek copies differ even over where to divide the following verse; and add that whatever degree of knowledge has been attained is to be retained and not departed from.

Fill in the usage of the disputed word from elsewhere, where it marks those who are grown men rather than children in understanding, adults in Christian knowledge, thoroughly instructed and experienced, and gloss it here as fit for the race and strong in faith; attach the promise of revelation to sincerity, since those who are upright will be given full instruction in these divine things; report that the manuscripts, versions and fathers of the Alexandrian text omit the closing words about the rule and the same mind, that the disagreement among copies is wide enough for most critics to treat them as a gloss never original, and that one editor pronounced them most certainly to be deleted; and warn against losing the ground already gained.

Turn the passage into a rule of forbearance: this is the thing wherein all good Christians are agreed, to make Christ all in all and set their hearts on another world, however they may differ in their sentiments about other things; and therefore those who differ over meats and days and other matters of the Jewish law must not judge one another, since they meet now in Christ as their centre and hope to meet shortly in heaven as their home. Lay no great stress on such differences, wait till God gives a better understanding, and in the meantime go together as far as you have attained, joining in all the great things on which you are agreed.

debates.question: Who are the perfect addressed here?

sides.position: Those who would be perfect or are aiming at it, since he can hardly address as perfect what he has just refused to call himself
Spiritual adults, the term meaning relative perfection in contrast to the absolute perfection just denied
Those who held themselves already to have attained, the word being used with a touch of irony

debates.question: Are the closing words of the sixteenth verse original?

sides.position: No: the Alexandrian manuscripts, versions and fathers omit them, most critics treat them as a gloss never original, and one editor pronounced them most certainly to be deleted
No: they are an explanatory gloss, partly taken from the end of Galatians
The word for rule is absent from the oldest witnesses
The Greek copies differ even over where the clauses should be divided

outliers.note: Alone frames the address as a paradox, that those who hold themselves perfect are bidden to prove it by a consciousness of imperfection, and that if they lack it they have something yet to learn.

Alone draws the pastoral inference that we must bear for a time with ignorance in weaker brethren, noting that the apostle was entirely assured of his own doctrine yet allowed those who could not receive it time to make progress.

themes: God shall reveal even this unto you
let us walk by the same rule

17.pericope_label: Brethren, be followers together of me, and mark them which walk so as ye have us for an ensample. (For many walk, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, that they are the enemies of the cross of Christ: Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.) For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.

schools.summary: Note that the word for following is peculiar, signifying not simply follow me but unite in following me, so that the example serves unity as well as rectitude, and that the verb for marking others means to keep the eyes on them as a goal, here to follow rather than to avoid; identify the enemies of the cross with an Antinomian party sheltering its profligacy under the preaching of liberty, or else leave the Judaising and the Epicurean identifications open as alternatives; explain that the word rendered conversation means the administration of a state and then the community itself, so that two societies are set against each other, one governed by worldly laws and one by the laws of heaven; prefer our city to our citizenship on grammar and usage, and press the local point that as the inhabitants of a Roman colony were citizens of a far distant imperial city so these readers were already citizens of the better country; and correct the familiar rendering of the last verse, since the body is not really vile but is the body of our humiliation, humiliation being only its outward fashion.

Remove the suspicion of ambition from the call to imitation, since it is all one whom they single out provided they conform to the purity of which he was a pattern, a man devoted to his own interests wishing to have no rival; take the tears as evidence that no envy or hatred or disposition to revile moved him but pious zeal at seeing the church destroyed by such pests; canvass the explanations of others as to who the enemies are and settle on a general reading, that these were not open adversaries but impostors who trampled the power of the gospel for the sake of ambition or of their own belly, and did more injury than if they had opposed Christ outright; and measure the promised glory by the transfiguration, asking who could bear its fullness when the disciples could not endure the slight taste afforded there.

Make the incongruity the whole point, that nothing is so foreign to a Christian as to seek ease and rest, and to be engrossed with the present life is foreign to our profession and enlistment: thy Master was crucified, and dost thou seek ease; thy Master was pierced with nails, and dost thou live delicately; do these things become a noble soldier? Those who made a pretence of Christianity yet lived in ease and luxury are for that reason enemies of the cross, since did they love it they would strive to live the crucified life; and take up the cross not merely by sealing yourself with it but by suffering the things belonging to it, the sufferings themselves being what the Master called by that name.

Observe that there are many called by Christ's name who are enemies to his cross, and that their walk is a surer evidence of what they are than their profession; note that the warning is repeated because we so little heed the warnings given us, and that an old sermon may be preached with new affections, this being a weeping preacher as Jeremiah was a weeping prophet; then give the characters — a wretched idol it is when the same observance which good people give to God is given by epicures to their appetites; they boast of what should have been their shame; and by minding earthly things they act directly against the design of the cross, which came to crucify the world to us and us to the world.

Keep the stadium in view to the end, letting the writings, preaching and conduct be the line and the eye stay fixed on those who walk by it; identify the enemies flatly as the Judaizing teachers, who attribute justification to the Levitical sacrifices rather than to the sacrificial death of Christ, please the world and are in no danger of reproach; set out their three characters, that they live only for time and make a gain of godliness, that they treat as a proof of their address the sumptuous living got by flattering the passions of their hearers, and that their whole study is taken up with earthly matters; and read the citizenship against them, since they have no city but what is on earth and no rights but what are derived from their secular connections.

debates.question: Who are the enemies of the cross of Christ?

sides.position: The Judaizing teachers, who attribute justification to the Levitical sacrifices, please the world and are in no danger of reproach
Men who made a pretence of Christianity yet lived in ease and luxury, which is contrary to the cross
An Antinomian party sheltering its profligacy under the preaching of liberty, accepting the cross Christ bore while refusing the cross we are to take up
Either the Judaizers or Epicurean antinomians — both identifications stand open
Not open adversaries but impostors and profligates who trampled the power of the gospel for ambition or for their own belly

debates.question: Does the word rendered conversation mean our citizenship or our city?

sides.position: Our city, on both the grammatical form and the ordinary usage of the word
The community or commonwealth to which we belong, so that two societies are set against each other
Citizenship, as the inscriptions use it, though the rendering we are a colony of heaven reverses the relation between colony and mother city
Our city, or citizenship, or civil rights — properly the administration or form of a republic

debates.question: In what sense is the body changed?

sides.position: In its qualities and not in its substance or its form and figure, which remain the same, as with the Lord's body after the resurrection
In its fashion only, humiliation being the outward vesture of the body, which is fallen and degraded but not really vile
Into a body adapted to the glorified world, of the same nature as the spiritual bodies of the saints in the resurrection

outliers.note: Alone divides the doctrine of the cross into two parts, the one Christ bore alone which we can only believe, and the one we are to take up and follow him in, so that men who accept the first may still be enemies of the second.
Alone reports Milligan’s doubt whether the rendering a colony of heaven is defensible, since it reverses the relation between the colony and the mother city.

themes: enemies of the cross of Christ
